full_judgment:
4. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are briefly stated below; Plaintiff opposite party No.1 Md. Shahadat Hossain filed the above noted suit claiming that the suit land measuring 2.50 acres belonged to her maternal grandmother Soleman Nessa. Defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are the three daughters of Soleman Nessa. Two of these daughters, being defendant Nos. 1 and 3, were given in marriage and they used to live at different villages with their respective husbands. The other daughter Defendant No.2 and her husband being plaintiff's mother and father respectively and plaintiff himself live at the house of Soleman Nessa. Plaintiff used to look after Soleman Nessa and he delivered to her a copy of the holy Quran and a bunch of tasbih. So, out of love and affection, Soleman Nessa executed a deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz on 2-4-1986 at the local Sub Registry office and thereby transferred the suit land to the plaintiff. However the deed could not be presented for registration, because after execution of the deed the office was closed. Subsequently the grand mother Soleman Nessa became ill and ultimately died on 4-5-1986. However the transfer was completed by way of delivery of the Ewaz and delivery of possession of the land. But registration of the deed could not be completed because of the death of the executant Soleman Nessa. So plaintiff requested his mother and maternal aunts being the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 for registration of deed of the Heba-bil- Ewaz, but they refused. Hence the suit for specific performance of contract. 

 5. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3, being the two daughters of Soleman Nessa and defendant Nos. 5 and 6 being the two purchasers from the said two daughters contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. They admitted that the suit land belonged to Soleman Nessa. But they have denied the execution of the deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz. Their case is that plaintiff has created a false and forged deed and that after the death of Soleman Nessa her property devolved upon defendant Nos. 1-3 being her three daughters and two of these daughters being defendant Nos. 1 and 3 sold 1.58 acres of land out of the suit land by four registered sale deeds dated 28-6-1986 in favour of defendant No.5 and 6 who are in possession of this land. 

 17. On perusal of the impugned judgment of the appellate Court and that of the trial Court, it appears that both the courts below found that the disputed deed was duly executed as stated by PW 1 and corroborated by the local witnesses (PW 2, 3 and 4). 

 18. The Courts below, with reference to the statements of the PWs and also to those of the DWs, found that the plaintiff's grandmother used to live with and was looked after by, the plaintiff. The courts below also found that the deed in question was a contractual document and therefore enforceable in a suit for specific performance of contract. 

 19. Against the backdrop stated above, the issues before this court are threefold: 20. Firstly, whether a deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz is contractual document and, if so, whether registration thereof is necessary as per law. 

 24. In the well-known book titled '' Principles of Mohammadan Law" written by DF Mollah, edit- edby M. Hedayetullah and Arshad Hedayetullah, Section 168 19th Edition, reference has been made to Baillie and Macnaghten, and the relevant principles regarding the legal nature of a deed of Heba-bil- Ewaz are stated as follows (underlines added): 

 30. These kind of transfers have been taking place in this country for a long time and have been mentioned in at least one statue i.e. in section 96(10) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. According to that provision certain gift or Heba are exempted from pre-emption, but not a "Heba-bil- Ewaz for pecuniary consideration". 

 35. It is noted that defendant Nos. 2, the other daughter of Soleman Nessa and mother of the plaintiff, did not file any written statement, nor was she produced by the plaintiff or the contesting defendants as a witness. 

 37. As stated earlier, both the Courts below assessed and analyses the oral evidence of the witnesses, particularly the statements of PW. 1, 2, 3 and 4 and came to the conclusion that the disputed Heba-bil-Ewaz was duly executed after receipt of Ewaz. 

 38. However the issue raised in the revision is about non consideration of material evidence, particularly the LTI of Soleman Nessa on the disputed deed. In this respect the plaintiff (PW 1) Md. Shahadat Hossain, being the transferee stated as follows. 

 39. PW 2 Md. Doulat Hossain is the attesting witness. He stated about execution of the document as follows (under lines added): 

 40. PW 3 Md. Abu Yousuf Sheikh, stated about delivery of the Quran and Tasbih by the plaintiff to Soleman Nessa in presence of PW 3 himself and the three daughters of Soleman Nessa, and others. This witness also stated about existing possession of the plaintiff (PW1) over the suit land. 

 41. PW 4. Md. Younus Ali is the scribe of the document, and his statement made in examination in chief with regard to execution is quoted below: 

 42. So from the statements of PW 1 the plaintiff, and transferee the attesting witnesses PW 2 and the scribe PW.4, as quoted above, it is evident that, according to them, the deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz was written first, and then it was read over to, and the LTI was put on the document, by the executant Soleman Nessa. 

 43. But these statements do not conform to the contents of Exhibit-1 being the original deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz. For proper appreciation of the fact in issue of due execution by Soleman Nessa the location of her L TI on the 1st and 2nd pages are to be examined. The relevant portion of those two pages are produced below as scanned image/photographs (by using the electronic Scanner machine and the computer): 

 44. This aspect of the location of the LTI on the second page of Exhibit 1 compared to that of the first page or other pages were not at all noticed by the trial Court or by the appellate Court. Even during the first time hearing of this revision, this aspect was not noticed by myself or by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, and the judgment was pronounced discharging the Rule. But before signing the judgment, I noticed this aspect. So the matter was fixed for rehearing and it was pointed out to the learned Advocates for both sides and they made their respective submission as stated earlier. The unsigned judgment was recalled. 

 46. This failure of the plaintiff to prove the due execution of the disputed deed is further reinforced by the statement of PW.1 being the transferee (donee) himself: He stated that the document could not be presented for registration on 2-4-1986 as the office time was over, and that subsequently the executant fell ill and that she could not be taken to the Sub-Registry office for the purpose of registration. According to the plaint she died after about one month i.e. on 4-5-1986 

 48. The submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party (plaintiff) with regard to remand is not acceptable in-view of the fact that the evidence on record is sufficient to come to a conclusion about the due execution. The PW's have made statements in their own way and these statements are found to be clearly contradictory to the location of the LTI on page-2 of the document which clearly shows that the document was written after the LTI was taken and therefore it was not a due execution. So the remand of the case would riot yield anything new or better result that might help proper adjudication of the dispute. 

 "7. A perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division shows that the learned Single Judge found that there are misreading of evidences and that both the courts below have not at all considered the material evidence on record and for that he sent the case back on remand. It is to be stated here that if there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the " material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case".
